rationale:
SPLIT into 6 independent children. Each is a standard, reusable fact. None depends on a sibling.
- Step 1 → pairing_upper_bound.
- Step 2 → compact_inner_approx.
- Step 4 → open_outer_approx.
- Step 5 → vector_lusin.
- Steps 6–7 → unit_field_extension.
- Step 8 → pairing_lower_bound.
The parent keeps only steps 3 and 9 and the choice of a Borel version ν₀.

ASSEMBLY (the parent's own proof). Write S for the supremum.

(S ≤ μ(O)): use iSup_le with pairing_upper_bound. O is measurable because it is open, and |ν| ≤ 1 a.e. follows from |ν| = 1 a.e.

(μ(O) ≤ S):
1. compact_inner_approx with c := S reduces to μ(K) ≤ S for each compact K ⊆ O.
2. By ENNReal.le_of_forall_pos_le_add, fix ε > 0 and set η := ε/3.
3. open_outer_approx gives an open V with K ⊆ V ⊆ O, μ(V) < ∞ and μ(V∖K) < η.
4. Let ν₀ := AEStronglyMeasurable.mk ν. It is Borel and ν = ν₀ μ-a.e. Set A := K ∩ {|ν₀| = 1}. A is Borel, μ(A) < ∞, and μ(K∖A) = 0.
5. vector_lusin on (μ, ν₀, A, η) gives a closed C ⊆ A with μ(A∖C) < η and ν₀ continuous on C. C is compact, being closed inside K.
6. unit_field_extension on (C, V, ν₀) gives an admissible g with tsupport g ⊆ V ⊆ O and g = ν₀ on C. Hence ofReal(∫⟨g,ν⟩) ≤ S.
7. For μ-a.e. x ∈ C, ⟨g(x),ν(x)⟩ = |ν₀(x)|² = 1, and g = 0 off V. pairing_lower_bound then gives μ(C) ≤ ofReal(∫⟨g,ν⟩) + μ(V∖C).
8. μ(K∖C) ≤ μ(K∖A) + μ(A∖C) < η and μ(V∖C) ≤ μ(V∖K) + μ(K∖C) < 2η. So μ(K) ≤ μ(C) + μ(K∖C) ≤ S + 3η = S + ε (ENNReal.add_thirds).
9. Conclude with le_antisymm.

Parent N = 0 case: needs no special treatment, because A = ∅ there and every child is uniform in N.

Small specialisations of the parent argument:
- Urysohn is applied to C rather than K. Only χ = 1 on K' is used in step 8.
- Child 3 returns the open V directly; the compact L of the parent is internal to its proof.

subproblems.title: The pairing of a unit field supported in O with a field ν with |ν| ≤ 1 a.e. is at most μ(O)
subproblems.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ, write ℝ^N for EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N) with its Euclidean norm and inner product, and let μ be any measure on the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ^N. Let O ⊆ ℝ^N be a Borel set. Let ν, g : ℝ^N → ℝ^N be arbitrary maps (no measurability is assumed) such that |ν(x)| ≤ 1 for μ-a.e. x, tsupport g (the closure of {g ≠ 0}) is contained in O, and |g(x)| ≤ 1 for every x. Then ofReal(∫⟨g(x), ν(x)⟩ dμ(x)) ≤ μ(O) in [0, ∞]. Here ∫ is the Bochner integral, which is 0 when the integrand is not μ-integrable, and ofReal(t) := max(t, 0).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (O : Set (Rn N)) (μ : Measure (Rn N)) (ν g : Rn N → Rn N), MeasurableSet O → (∀ᵐ x ∂μ, ‖ν x‖ ≤ 1) → tsupport g ⊆ O → (∀ x, ‖g x‖ ≤ 1) → ENNReal.ofReal (∫ x, inner ℝ (g x) (ν x) ∂μ) ≤ μ O
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. This is step 1 of the parent proof (S ≤ μ(O)), for a single field g. The parent bounds |⟨g, ν⟩| a.e. by the indicator of tsupport g ⊆ O and then integrates. Here the same a.e. bound is taken against the indicator of O and integrated with the lower Lebesgue integral. That route needs no integrability, measurability or compact-support hypothesis, which is why the statement has none.

Notation. f(x) := ⟨g(x), ν(x)⟩ ∈ ℝ. For t ∈ ℝ, ‖t‖ₑ := ofReal(|t|) ∈ [0, ∞) is the extended norm of t. 1_O : ℝ^N → [0, ∞] is the indicator function of O.

1. A.e. pointwise bound. We claim ‖f(x)‖ₑ ≤ 1_O(x) for μ-a.e. x. Fix x in the μ-full set where |ν(x)| ≤ 1.
 (a) Suppose x ∈ O. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, |f(x)| ≤ |g(x)| |ν(x)| ≤ 1 · 1 = 1. Hence ‖f(x)‖ₑ = ofReal(|f(x)|) ≤ ofReal(1) = 1 = 1_O(x).
 (b) Suppose x ∉ O. Since tsupport g ⊆ O, x ∉ tsupport g. Since support g ⊆ tsupport g, g(x) = 0 (Mathlib image_eq_zero_of_notMem_tsupport). Then f(x) = ⟨0, ν(x)⟩ = 0 and ‖f(x)‖ₑ = 0 = 1_O(x).
2. For every real t, t ≤ |t| and ofReal is monotone, so ofReal(t) ≤ ofReal(|t|) = ‖t‖ₑ (Real.enorm_eq_ofReal_abs). Taking t := ∫ f dμ gives ofReal(∫ f dμ) ≤ ‖∫ f dμ‖ₑ.
3. ‖∫ f dμ‖ₑ ≤ ∫⁻ ‖f(x)‖ₑ dμ(x). This holds with no hypothesis on f (Mathlib enorm_integral_le_lintegral_enorm). If f is not μ-integrable, the Bochner integral is 0 and the left side is 0. Otherwise this is the triangle inequality for the Bochner integral.
4. By step 1 and monotonicity of the lower integral under μ-a.e. inequalities (lintegral_mono_ae), ∫⁻ ‖f‖ₑ dμ ≤ ∫⁻ 1_O dμ. Since O is measurable, ∫⁻ 1_O dμ = μ(O) (lintegral_indicator_one).
5. Chaining steps 2, 3 and 4 gives ofReal(∫⟨g, ν⟩ dμ) ≤ ‖∫ f dμ‖ₑ ≤ ∫⁻ ‖f‖ₑ dμ ≤ μ(O). ∎
proof_key_steps: For μ-a.e. x, |⟨g(x), ν(x)⟩| ≤ 1_O(x): Cauchy–Schwarz gives the bound on O, and off O we have x ∉ tsupport g, so g(x) = 0.
ofReal(∫f) ≤ ‖∫f‖ₑ ≤ ∫⁻‖f‖ₑ dμ, with no integrability needed.
∫⁻‖f‖ₑ dμ ≤ ∫⁻ 1_O dμ = μ(O) because O is measurable.

subproblems.title: The measure of an open set is bounded by any common bound on its compact subsets
subproblems.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ, let O ⊆ ℝ^N (= EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N)) be open, let μ be any measure on the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ^N (no finiteness is assumed), and let c ∈ [0, ∞]. If μ(K) ≤ c for every compact K ⊆ O, then μ(O) ≤ c. In other words, μ(O) = sup{μ(K) : K ⊆ O compact}.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (O : Set (Rn N)) (μ : Measure (Rn N)) (c : ℝ≥0∞), IsOpen O → (∀ K : Set (Rn N), IsCompact K → K ⊆ O → μ K ≤ c) → μ O ≤ c
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. This is step 2 of the parent proof (reduction to compact sets: O is σ-compact and μ is continuous from below). Compare Simon Ch. 1, Remark 1.16 (chapter-01.txt lines 287–295), where a closed subset of a σ-compact space is written as an increasing union of compact sets.

1. Closed exhaustion. O is an open subset of the metric space ℝ^N, so there are closed sets F_0 ⊆ F_1 ⊆ F_2 ⊆ … with F_n ⊆ O for every n and ⋃_n F_n = O. For example, if O = ℝ^N take F_n := ℝ^N. Otherwise take F_n := {x : dist(x, ℝ^N ∖ O) ≥ 1/(n+1)}:
- F_n is closed because x ↦ dist(x, ℝ^N ∖ O) is continuous.
- F_n ⊆ O because points of the closed set ℝ^N ∖ O have distance 0.
- F_n increases with n.
- The F_n exhaust O, because each x ∈ O has a ball around it inside O and therefore positive distance to ℝ^N ∖ O.
Mathlib's IsOpen.exists_iUnion_isClosed provides such a monotone family.
2. Compact exhaustion. Put K_n := F_n ∩ B̄(0, n), where B̄(0, n) = {x : |x| ≤ n}.
- K_n is closed and bounded in ℝ^N, so it is compact (Heine–Borel: a closed subset of the compact ball; isCompact_closedBall with IsCompact.inter_left).
- K_n ⊆ F_n ⊆ O.
- If m ≤ n, then F_m ⊆ F_n and B̄(0, m) ⊆ B̄(0, n), so K_m ⊆ K_n.
3. ⋃_n K_n = O. The inclusion ⊆ follows from step 2. Conversely, let x ∈ O. Choose n with x ∈ F_n (step 1) and m ∈ ℕ with m ≥ |x| (Archimedean property). With p := max(n, m), x ∈ F_n ⊆ F_p and |x| ≤ m ≤ p, so x ∈ K_p.
4. Continuity from below. For any measure and any increasing sequence of sets, μ(⋃_n K_n) = sup_n μ(K_n) (Mathlib Monotone.measure_iUnion, which needs no measurability; here the K_n are closed anyway). With step 3, μ(O) = sup_n μ(K_n).
5. Each K_n is a compact subset of O, so μ(K_n) ≤ c by hypothesis. Therefore μ(O) = sup_n μ(K_n) ≤ c. ∎
proof_key_steps: O = ⋃_n F_n with closed, increasing F_n ⊆ O.
K_n := F_n ∩ B̄(0, n) are compact, increasing, contained in O, and ⋃_n K_n = O.
Continuity from below gives μ(O) = sup_n μ(K_n) ≤ c.

subproblems.title: A compact K ⊆ O has an open neighbourhood V ⊆ O of finite measure with μ(V ∖ K) < ε
subproblems.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ, let O ⊆ ℝ^N (= EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N)) be open, let K ⊆ O be compact, and let μ be a measure on the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ^N with μ(L) < ∞ for every compact L ⊆ O. Then for every ε ∈ (0, ∞] there is an open set V ⊆ ℝ^N with K ⊆ V ⊆ O, μ(V) < ∞ and μ(V ∖ K) < ε.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (O K : Set (Rn N)) (μ : Measure (Rn N)), IsOpen O → IsCompact K → K ⊆ O → (∀ L : Set (Rn N), IsCompact L → L ⊆ O → μ L < ∞) → ∀ ε : ℝ≥0∞, 0 < ε → ∃ V : Set (Rn N), IsOpen V ∧ K ⊆ V ∧ V ⊆ O ∧ μ V < ∞ ∧ μ (V \ K) < ε
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. This is step 4 of the parent proof. There, a compact neighbourhood L of K with μ(L ∖ K) < ε is built from thickenings by continuity from above, together with an open V with K ⊆ V ⊆ L. Here continuity from above is applied directly to the open thickenings, which yields V at once.

1. A compact neighbourhood inside O. There is δ₀ > 0 with L₀ := {x : dist(x, K) ≤ δ₀} ⊆ O (Mathlib IsCompact.exists_cthickening_subset_open). If K = ∅ then L₀ = ∅, and if O = ℝ^N any δ₀ > 0 works. Otherwise x ↦ dist(x, ℝ^N ∖ O) is continuous and positive on the nonempty compact K, so it has a minimum 2δ₀ > 0 there. If dist(x, K) ≤ δ₀, compactness gives k ∈ K with |x − k| ≤ δ₀. Then dist(x, ℝ^N ∖ O) ≥ 2δ₀ − δ₀ > 0, so x ∈ O. L₀ is closed and bounded, hence compact (IsCompact.cthickening), and L₀ ⊆ O, so μ(L₀) < ∞ by hypothesis. Likewise μ(K) < ∞, because K is a compact subset of O.
2. Open thickenings. For r > 0 let V_r := {x : dist(x, K) < r} (Mathlib Metric.thickening r K; V_r = ∅ if K = ∅). Then:
- V_r is open (Metric.isOpen_thickening).
- K ⊆ V_r, since points of K have distance 0 < r (Metric.self_subset_thickening).
- V_r ⊆ V_s whenever r ≤ s.
- V_r ⊆ L₀ whenever r ≤ δ₀ (Metric.thickening_subset_cthickening_of_le).
3. Continuity from above. K is closed (compact in a Hausdorff space), so ⋂_{r>0} V_r = closure K = K. Since μ(V_{δ₀}) ≤ μ(L₀) < ∞, continuity from above along the decreasing family V_r gives μ(V_r) → μ(K) as r ↓ 0 (Mathlib tendsto_measure_thickening_of_isClosed). Concretely, μ(V_{δ₀/m}) ↓ μ(K) as m → ∞, and r ↦ μ(V_r) is monotone.
4. Choice of V. Since μ(K) < ∞ and ε > 0, μ(K) < μ(K) + ε (ENNReal.lt_add_right). By step 3 there is r with 0 < r < δ₀ and μ(V_r) < μ(K) + ε. Put V := V_r.
5. Verification.
- V is open and K ⊆ V, by step 2.
- V ⊆ L₀ ⊆ O because r ≤ δ₀.
- μ(V) ≤ μ(L₀) < ∞.
- K ⊆ V, K is Borel (closed) and μ(K) < ∞, so μ(V ∖ K) = μ(V) − μ(K) < ε (Mathlib measure_sdiff and ENNReal.sub_lt_of_lt_add, using μ(V) < μ(K) + ε). ∎
proof_key_steps: Some closed δ₀-neighbourhood L₀ of K is compact and contained in O, so μ(L₀) < ∞ and μ(K) < ∞.
The open r-neighbourhoods V_r of K are open, contain K, lie in L₀ for r ≤ δ₀, and decrease to K as r ↓ 0, so μ(V_r) → μ(K) by continuity from above.
Choose r ∈ (0, δ₀) with μ(V_r) < μ(K) + ε. Then V := V_r works, with μ(V ∖ K) = μ(V) − μ(K) < ε.

subproblems.title: Lusin's theorem for ℝ^N-valued Borel maps on a set of finite μ-measure
subproblems.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ, let μ be a measure on the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ^N (= EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N)); no local finiteness is assumed. Let f : ℝ^N → ℝ^N be Borel measurable, let A ⊆ ℝ^N be a Borel set with μ(A) < ∞, and let ε ∈ (0, ∞]. Then there is a closed set C ⊆ ℝ^N with C ⊆ A, μ(A ∖ C) < ε, and f continuous on C (i.e. the restriction f|C is continuous).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Rn N)) (f : Rn N → Rn N) (A : Set (Rn N)), Measurable f → MeasurableSet A → μ A ≠ ∞ → ∀ ε : ℝ≥0∞, 0 < ε → ∃ C ⊆ A, IsClosed C ∧ μ (A \ C) < ε ∧ ContinuousOn f C
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. This is step 5 of the parent proof: Lusin's theorem applied coordinatewise to the finite Borel measure μ⌞A.
- Lusin's theorem: Simon Ch. 1, Theorem 1.17, chapter-01.txt lines 346–372. For real-valued functions it is formalized as SimonGMT Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.exists_isClosed_continuousOn_of_measurable in Poincare/SimonGMT/Chapter01/Lusin.lean. That module is not in the import closure of GMT.Ch03.Submission, so add `import Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.Lusin`.
- Regularity: finite Borel measures on metric spaces are closed-inner-regular (Simon Ch. 1, Theorem 1.15(2), chapter-01.txt lines 274–343).
- Generalizations of the parent argument: A is an arbitrary Borel set of finite measure and f an arbitrary Borel map. An extra closed set F is intersected in so that N = 0 needs no separate case.

1. The restricted measure. Let ρ := μ⌞A, i.e. ρ(S) := μ(S ∩ A) for Borel S. Then ρ(ℝ^N) = μ(A) < ∞, so ρ is a finite Borel measure on the metric space ℝ^N. For every Borel S ⊆ A, ρ(S) = μ(S).
2. Closed inner regularity of ρ. For every Borel S and every δ > 0 there is a closed F ⊆ S with ρ(S ∖ F) < δ. This is Simon Ch. 1, Theorem 1.15(2) for the finite measure ρ: in a metric space every closed set is a countable intersection of open sets. In Mathlib, ρ is weakly regular (Measure.WeaklyRegular.of_pseudoMetrizableSpace_of_isFiniteMeasure, with IsFiniteMeasure ρ from isFiniteMeasure_restrict), and MeasurableSet.exists_isClosed_sdiff_lt gives F.
3. Choice of δ. Since ε > 0, choose a real δ > 0 with (N + 1)·δ < ε. If ε = ∞, any δ > 0 works. Otherwise take δ := ε/(2(N + 1)). (Mathlib ENNReal.exists_pos_mul_lt gives δ with δ·(N + 1) < ε.)
4. A closed subset of A. By step 2 with S = A, there is a closed F ⊆ A with ρ(A ∖ F) < δ.
5. Coordinates. For i = 1, …, N let f^i(x) := f(x)_i be the i-th coordinate. f^i : ℝ^N → ℝ is Borel, as the composition of f with the continuous coordinate projection (EuclideanSpace.proj i). Apply Lusin's theorem for real functions to ρ, the Borel set A with ρ(A) < ∞, the function f^i and the tolerance δ. Its regularity hypothesis is exactly step 2. This gives a closed C_i ⊆ A with ρ(A ∖ C_i) < δ such that f^i is continuous on C_i.
6. Definition of C. Put C := F ∩ C_1 ∩ … ∩ C_N. C is closed as a finite intersection of closed sets, and C ⊆ F ⊆ A. When N = 0 there are no C_i and C = F; intersecting with F guarantees C ⊆ A in all cases.
7. Measure estimate. If x ∈ A ∖ C, then x ∉ F or x ∉ C_i for some i, so A ∖ C ⊆ (A ∖ F) ∪ ⋃_{i=1}^N (A ∖ C_i). All of these are Borel subsets of A, so by step 1 and subadditivity
 μ(A ∖ C) = ρ(A ∖ C) ≤ ρ(A ∖ F) + Σ_{i=1}^N ρ(A ∖ C_i) < δ + N·δ = (N + 1)·δ < ε.
8. Continuity. Each f^i is continuous on C, since C ⊆ C_i and f^i is continuous on C_i. The coordinate map z ↦ (z_1, …, z_N) is a linear homeomorphism from ℝ^N onto ℝ^{Fin N} (Mathlib EuclideanSpace.equiv). A map into a finite product is continuous on C iff each coordinate is (continuousOn_pi). So x ↦ (f^1(x), …, f^N(x)) is continuous on C, and composing with the inverse homeomorphism shows that f is continuous on C. ∎
proof_key_steps: ρ := μ⌞A is a finite Borel measure on a metric space, so every Borel set contains a closed set of nearly full ρ-measure.
Fix δ > 0 with (N+1)δ < ε. Take a closed F ⊆ A with ρ(A∖F) < δ, and by real Lusin closed C_i ⊆ A with ρ(A∖C_i) < δ and f^i continuous on C_i.
C := F ∩ C_1 ∩ … ∩ C_N is closed, C ⊆ A, and μ(A∖C) = ρ(A∖C) ≤ ρ(A∖F) + Σ_i ρ(A∖C_i) < (N+1)δ < ε.
Every coordinate of f is continuous on C, so f is continuous on C.

subproblems.title: Tietze–Urysohn: a field continuous on compact C ⊆ V with |f| ≤ 1 extends to a compactly supported continuous unit field in V
subproblems.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ and ℝ^N = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N). Let C ⊆ ℝ^N be compact, let V ⊆ ℝ^N be open with C ⊆ V, and let f : ℝ^N → ℝ^N be continuous on C with |f(x)| ≤ 1 for all x ∈ C. Then there is a continuous g : ℝ^N → ℝ^N such that g has compact support, tsupport g ⊆ V, |g(x)| ≤ 1 for every x ∈ ℝ^N, and g(x) = f(x) for every x ∈ C.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (C V : Set (Rn N)) (f : Rn N → Rn N), IsCompact C → IsOpen V → C ⊆ V → ContinuousOn f C → (∀ x ∈ C, ‖f x‖ ≤ 1) → ∃ g : Rn N → Rn N, Continuous g ∧ HasCompactSupport g ∧ tsupport g ⊆ V ∧ (∀ x, ‖g x‖ ≤ 1) ∧ ∀ x ∈ C, g x = f x
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. These are steps 6 (Tietze extension and radial retraction) and 7 (Urysohn cut-off) of the parent proof. The parent's closed set K' is renamed C. The cut-off is taken equal to 1 on C; in the parent it is 1 on K ⊇ K', but only χ = 1 on K' is used afterwards.

1. Topology. C is compact in the Hausdorff space ℝ^N, hence closed. ℝ^N is a metric space, hence normal, and it is locally compact Hausdorff.
2. Tietze extension. For i = 1, …, N, the coordinate x ↦ f(x)_i is a real function continuous on the closed set C. By the Tietze extension theorem it has a continuous extension G₁^i : ℝ^N → ℝ with G₁^i(x) = f(x)_i for x ∈ C. Put G₁ := (G₁^1, …, G₁^N) : ℝ^N → ℝ^N. G₁ is continuous and G₁ = f on C.
3. Radial retraction. Let r(z) := z / max(1, |z|) for z ∈ ℝ^N.
- r is continuous, since z ↦ max(1, |z|) is continuous and ≥ 1.
- |r(z)| = |z| / max(1, |z|) ≤ 1.
- r(z) = z when |z| ≤ 1.
Put G := r ∘ G₁. Then G is continuous and |G(x)| ≤ 1 for all x. For x ∈ C, G(x) = r(f(x)) = f(x), because |f(x)| ≤ 1.
Lean shortcut for steps 2–3: the closed unit ball B̄(0, 1) ⊆ ℝ^N has the Tietze extension property (Mathlib instance Set.instTietzeExtensionUnitClosedBall in Mathlib/Analysis/Complex/Tietze.lean). That module is not in the import closure of GMT.Ch03.Submission, so add `import Mathlib.Analysis.Complex.Tietze`. Apply ContinuousMap.exists_forall_mem_restrict_eq to the closed set C and the continuous map C → ℝ^N, x ↦ f(x) (continuous by ContinuousOn.domRestrict), whose values lie in B̄(0, 1). This yields a continuous G : ℝ^N → ℝ^N with G(x) ∈ B̄(0, 1) for all x and G = f on C.
4. Urysohn cut-off. ℝ^N is locally compact Hausdorff, C is compact, V is open and C ⊆ V. So there is a continuous χ : ℝ^N → ℝ with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 on C, tsupport χ compact and tsupport χ ⊆ V (Mathlib exists_continuousMap_one_of_isCompact_subset_isOpen).
5. Definition and properties of g. Put g(x) := χ(x)·G(x).
 (a) g is continuous, as the product of the continuous scalar function χ and the continuous field G.
 (b) support g ⊆ support χ, hence tsupport g ⊆ tsupport χ ⊆ V (tsupport_smul_subset_left).
 (c) tsupport g is a closed subset of the compact set tsupport χ, hence compact; that is, g has compact support (HasCompactSupport.smul_right).
 (d) For every x, |g(x)| = |χ(x)|·|G(x)| ≤ 1·1 = 1.
 (e) For x ∈ C, χ(x) = 1 and G(x) = f(x), so g(x) = f(x). ∎
proof_key_steps: C is closed, and Tietze extends f|C coordinatewise to a continuous G₁ : ℝ^N → ℝ^N.
G := r ∘ G₁, with r(z) = z/max(1,|z|), is continuous, satisfies |G| ≤ 1, and equals f on C because |f| ≤ 1 there. Equivalently, use Tietze into the closed unit ball.
Urysohn gives a continuous χ with values in [0,1], χ = 1 on C, and compact tsupport χ ⊆ V.
g := χG is continuous, compactly supported in V, satisfies |g| ≤ 1, and equals f on C.

subproblems.title: Lower bound for the pairing: μ(C) ≤ ofReal(∫⟨g, ν⟩ dμ) + μ(V ∖ C)
subproblems.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ and ℝ^N = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N). Let μ be a measure on the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ^N. Let ν : ℝ^N → ℝ^N be μ-a.e. strongly measurable with |ν(x)| ≤ 1 for μ-a.e. x. Let g : ℝ^N → ℝ^N be continuous with |g(x)| ≤ 1 for every x. Let C ⊆ V ⊆ ℝ^N be Borel sets with μ(V) < ∞. Assume g(x) = 0 for every x ∉ V, and ⟨g(x), ν(x)⟩ = 1 for μ-a.e. x ∈ C. Then μ(C) ≤ ofReal(∫⟨g(x), ν(x)⟩ dμ(x)) + μ(V ∖ C) in [0, ∞], where ∫ is the Bochner integral and ofReal(t) := max(t, 0).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Rn N)) (ν g : Rn N → Rn N) (C V : Set (Rn N)), MeasurableSet C → MeasurableSet V → C ⊆ V → μ V ≠ ∞ → AEStronglyMeasurable ν μ → Continuous g → (∀ᵐ x ∂μ, ‖ν x‖ ≤ 1) → (∀ x, ‖g x‖ ≤ 1) → (∀ x, x ∉ V → g x = 0) → (∀ᵐ x ∂μ, x ∈ C → inner ℝ (g x) (ν x) = 1) → μ C ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (∫ x, inner ℝ (g x) (ν x) ∂μ) + μ (V \ C)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. This is step 8 of the parent proof: the estimate ∫⟨g, ν⟩ dμ ≥ μ(K') − μ(L ∖ K'). Here K' is renamed C. The set L outside which g vanishes is replaced by V; only g = 0 off V and μ(V) < ∞ are used. The conclusion is stated in [0, ∞].

Notation. f(x) := ⟨g(x), ν(x)⟩ ∈ ℝ. For a Borel set B, 1_B is its real-valued indicator, and μ_ℝ(B) := μ(B) ∈ [0, ∞) whenever μ(B) < ∞.

1. Measurability. g is continuous, hence strongly measurable. ν is μ-a.e. strongly measurable, and (u, v) ↦ ⟨u, v⟩ is continuous. Hence f is μ-a.e. strongly measurable. In Mathlib: continuous_inner.comp_aestronglyMeasurable applied to (hg.aestronglyMeasurable.prodMk hν), or AEStronglyMeasurable.inner from Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Function/StronglyMeasurable/Inner.lean.
2. A.e. bounds. Let G₀ be the μ-full set of points x with |ν(x)| ≤ 1 and (x ∈ C ⇒ f(x) = 1); it is the intersection of two μ-full sets. For x ∈ G₀:
- |f(x)| ≤ |g(x)|·|ν(x)| ≤ 1 by Cauchy–Schwarz.
- If x ∉ V, then g(x) = 0 and so f(x) = 0.
Hence |f| ≤ 1_V μ-a.e.
3. Integrability.
- Since μ(V) < ∞, 1_V is μ-integrable. By steps 1 and 2, f is μ-integrable by domination (Integrable.mono').
- C and V ∖ C are Borel subsets of V, so μ(C) ≤ μ(V) < ∞ and μ(V ∖ C) ≤ μ(V) < ∞.
- 1_C and 1_{V∖C} are integrable, with ∫ 1_C dμ = μ_ℝ(C) and ∫ 1_{V∖C} dμ = μ_ℝ(V ∖ C) (integral_indicator_one).
4. Pointwise lower bound. For x ∈ G₀ we show f(x) ≥ 1_C(x) − 1_{V∖C}(x).
 (a) If x ∈ C: f(x) = 1 = 1 − 0, since x ∉ V ∖ C.
 (b) If x ∈ V ∖ C: f(x) ≥ −|f(x)| ≥ −1 = 0 − 1.
 (c) If x ∉ V: x ∉ C because C ⊆ V, and x ∉ V ∖ C, and f(x) = 0 = 0 − 0.
5. Integration. The integral is monotone for integrable functions under a μ-a.e. inequality, and it is linear (integral_mono_ae, integral_sub'). Therefore
 μ_ℝ(C) − μ_ℝ(V ∖ C) = ∫ (1_C − 1_{V∖C}) dμ ≤ ∫ f dμ.
6. Passage to [0, ∞]. Since μ(C) < ∞, μ(C) = ofReal(μ_ℝ(C)). By step 5, μ_ℝ(C) ≤ ∫ f dμ + μ_ℝ(V ∖ C). Also:
- ofReal is monotone.
- ofReal(a + b) ≤ ofReal(a) + ofReal(b) for all real a, b (ENNReal.ofReal_add_le).
- ofReal(μ_ℝ(V ∖ C)) = μ(V ∖ C), since μ(V ∖ C) < ∞.
Therefore μ(C) = ofReal(μ_ℝ(C)) ≤ ofReal(∫ f dμ + μ_ℝ(V ∖ C)) ≤ ofReal(∫ f dμ) + μ(V ∖ C). ∎
proof_key_steps: f := ⟨g, ν⟩ is a.e. strongly measurable and |f| ≤ 1_V μ-a.e., so f is integrable because μ(V) < ∞.
μ-a.e., f ≥ 1_C − 1_{V∖C}: f = 1 on C, f ≥ −1 on V∖C, and f = 0 off V.
Integrating gives μ(C) − μ(V∖C) ≤ ∫ f dμ as real numbers.
Converting to [0, ∞] gives μ(C) = ofReal(μ(C)) ≤ ofReal(∫ f) + μ(V∖C).
